source.title: Unlearning That Lasts: Utility-Preserving, Robust, and Almost Irreversible Forgetting in LLMs
source.authors: N. Singh; Maximilian Mueller; Francesco Croce; Matthias Hein

page_placements.theme: Measurement artifacts in MCQ and attack-based evaluation (both forgetting and recovery)

record.tranche_reason: The study directly tests whether unlearned factual knowledge returns under benign fine-tuning and prompt reformulations. Its results qualify the claim: recovery varies by method and unlearning duration, and the proposed JensUn method shows less recovery in several tested settings.
record.gate_note: Rows capture the reported relearning results and the tabled accuracy results for paraphrase and in-context-retain evaluations. Prompt variants cited from earlier work, claims about other studies, and results shown only in figures are not recorded as numerical rows. The study does not test activation-direction ablation or weight quantization.
record.test_reason: The study runs benign-relearning attacks (B) on LKF and paraphrase and in-context-retain prompting attacks (E) on RWKU against several unlearning methods. It reports how much forgotten knowledge returns. It also proposes JensUn and tests a prior robust method (NPO+SAM) against relearning (F). Its main argument is that standard evaluations overestimate unlearning, and that relearning success depends on unlearning duration. This qualifies A and B, so T5 fits. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also state that benign relearning becomes ineffective for GradDiff and JensUn after 1000–2000 unlearning steps, contrary to Lucki et al. They attribute GradDiff's robustness to a broken model (WR 0.03), while NPO and NPO+SAM stay vulnerable. They read JensUn's low recovery as evidence of more genuine knowledge removal.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes JensUn, a Jensen-Shannon-divergence unlearning objective, and evaluates several existing methods with its own datasets and worst-case prompt protocol; it is not a replication of one of the named original methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery depends on unlearning method and duration. Prompt evaluation also varies with paraphrases and in-context retain examples; the combined worst-case is higher than either standard evaluation or individual prompt conditions in the reported comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing ROUGE with an LLM judge changes method rankings on RWKU and aligns better with human judgments (Table 7, Figure 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Measured unlearning success depends on the scoring metric; ROUGE misestimates factual forgetting.

fits_no_version.finding: Worst-case paraphrase and in-context evaluation raises accuracy of the never-unlearned model by 17–33 points (Table 8) and 31 points on LKF (Figure 12).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard single-query evaluations underestimate baseline knowledge, so part of apparent prompting 'recovery' is evaluation strength rather than shallow unlearning.

record.problems: Relearning is evaluated on LKF and with the described training setup; the 200-QA real-knowledge set is not a very small set. Relearning is run for 600 steps with settings selected to test recovery rather than preserve utility, and the authors state the relearnt models do not yield good utility. RWKU prompt-attack results are reported for a subset of methods. The paper reports occasional judge/API errors for RWKU evaluations and excludes affected samples.
record.rows_left_out: Within the 60-row cap, omitted separate primary unlearning/utility trade-off rows from Tables 1–2 and supplementary sweeps, other-model relearning or unlearning results, and additional prompt formulations or figure-only results. The retained rows prioritize the relearning outcomes and tabled prompt-attack comparisons relevant to versions A, B, E and F.

untested.parts: Entire version: no activation ablation or internal analysis.
Relearning on a subset of the forgotten facts (the authors explicitly exclude it), and relearning sets much smaller than 200 QA pairs.

Explicit jailbreaks and other-language prompts are not run by the authors. They only compare against RWKU's adversarial (AA) set, which includes translations and is not captured in rows. In-context information about the forgotten facts themselves is not tested.
JensUn and NPO+SAM are not tested against activation ablation, quantization or forget-set relearning. JensUn's prompting robustness is tested on RWKU only, without a standard baseline.
WMDP/hazardous-knowledge settings and models larger than 3.8B.

missing.what: RWKU adversarial (AA) set accuracy per method, which includes rephrases and other-language prompts (e.g. GradDiff AA 12.7 vs FB 4.8).
LKF standard vs worst-case forget accuracy for unlearned models; RMU is underestimated by up to 43 points (10%→46% in Fig 13).
RWKU worst-case forget accuracy after 10-epoch unlearning (e.g. JensUn 14.3 FB / 6.1 QA, GradDiff 18.7 / 9.2).
Phi-3 LKF results: GradDiff, NPO and JensUn worst-case accuracy 1–3 with WR 0.31–0.49; RMU and SimNPO 43–45.

record.verdict_notes: Relearning uses 600 steps with settings chosen to maximize recovery regardless of utility. The relearning set is 200 QA pairs, not tiny. Table 8 has no standard-evaluation baseline for JensUn. The record's A label on r31–r54 was invalid because those rows link only to E; A verdicts here use relearning rows only. Prompting gains for unlearned models should be read against the original model's comparable gains.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests factual accuracy under its evaluations and reports utility metrics, but does not establish a general chance-level criterion for all methods or settings.
The unrelated relearning set has 200 QA pairs; the study does not test extremely small sets or relearning on a subset of forgotten facts.
No activation-direction ablation or direct internal-mechanism test.
Tests paraphrases and retain-set examples placed in context. Does not test jailbreaks or other languages; its in-context examples are retain-set examples, not forgotten facts.
Tests JensUn against the study's benign fine-tuning and prompt-evaluation settings, not against activation-direction ablation or quantization.
